title: The N-Queens Problem
excerpt: Place n queens on an n by n board with none attacking another. The interesting part is not the search, it is the two reformulations that shrink it from 4 billion candidates to a few thousand.

content.text: Place eight queens on a chessboard so that no two attack each other. A queen covers her whole row, her whole column and both diagonals, so this is harder than it sounds and easier than it looks.

The puzzle is not new. The chess composer Max Bezzel published it in 1848, and Franz Nauck published the first solutions in 1850. Gauss worked on it too. It survives as a teaching problem because the search is small enough to watch and the pruning is dramatic enough to feel.

body.text: How big is the naive search?

content.text: Choosing 8 squares out of 64 gives 64 choose 8, which is 4,426,165,368 arrangements. Testing all of them is possible and pointless.
Two observations collapse that number, and neither is an algorithm. They are reformulations, which is usually where the real speedup in a backtracking problem comes from.

rows: Two queens cannot share a row, so put exactly one queen per row
Two queens cannot share a column either, so the assignment is a permutation
Reject a placement the moment it conflicts, rather than at the end

content.text: From four billion to a couple of thousand, and only the last row is backtracking. The first two are just noticing what the constraints already told you.
Switch the widget to "Place them yourself" and try to solve the 6 by 6 board without help. Nothing stops you putting two queens in one row, and it is worth doing that once to see the tool report it.

Then switch to "Watch it solve" and step through. Red squares are attacked by a queen already placed. A square marked with a cross is one the solver considered and rejected before building anything underneath it.

The moment to watch for is a row where every column is attacked. The solver has nothing to try, so it returns, lifts the queen from the row above, and continues from there. That is the backtrack, and on a 6 by 6 board it happens constantly.
Try n = 4 as well. It has only two solutions and they are mirror images, so the whole search is short enough to follow end to end without losing your place.
The number of solutions does not grow smoothly, which surprises people expecting something tidy.

headers: Unique up to rotation and reflection

content.text: Six has fewer solutions than five, which is a good reminder that these counts come from the structure of the board rather than from any formula worth memorising. There is no known closed form. The values above are from
Wikipedia's eight queens puzzle article
, which also covers the history and the symmetry classes.
The naive conflict test walks every previously placed queen. It is O(row) per check, which is fine, and there is a neater way that is O(1).
Two squares are on the same descending diagonal exactly when
row - col
matches, and on the same ascending diagonal when
row + col
matches. So three sets, one for columns and one for each diagonal direction, answer the question immediately.
Add
to the
row - col
value if you want to index an array rather than use a hash set. That is the usual competitive-programming form.

variants.code:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    solutions = []
    queens = []              # queens[row] = column
    cols, diag, anti = set(), set(), set()   # col, row - col, row + col

    def backtrack(row):
        if row == n:
            solutions.append(list(queens))
            return

        for col in range(n):
            # O(1) conflict test, no loop over placed queens.
            if col in cols or (row - col) in diag or (row + col) in anti:
                continue

            queens.append(col)                               # choose
            cols.add(col); diag.add(row - col); anti.add(row + col)

            backtrack(row + 1)                               # explore

            queens.pop()                                     # un-choose
            cols.discard(col); diag.discard(row - col); anti.discard(row + col)

    backtrack(0)
    return solutions


# len(solve_n_queens(8)) -> 92

content.text: Counting solutions stays feasible into the high twenties with good pruning and bitmask representations, and stops being feasible shortly after. There is no polynomial algorithm for counting them.

Finding a single solution is a different question, and much easier: there are direct constructions that place n non-attacking queens without any search at all. If a problem only needs one arrangement, searching for it is the wrong tool.
For the state of the art on the search side, Donald Knuth's
Dancing Links

paper is the standard reference. It reframes problems like this as exact cover and uses reversible operations on doubly linked lists to make the undo step nearly free, and the paper reports results for n-queens up to n = 18.

questions.prompt: Why does the solver place exactly one queen per row rather than choosing 8 squares from 64?

options.label: Two queens can never share a row, so the constraint is built into the representation
It makes the code shorter but does not affect the search size
Because queens move differently along rows than columns

content.text: The widget shows the search running, but it is worth reading the first stretch of it written out, because the backtracks are where the algorithm earns its name and they go past quickly on screen.
Columns are lettered a to d, rows numbered 1 to 4. The solver fills one row at a time, top down.

 2. Row 2: try a -> rejected, a1 shares the column
 3. Row 2: try b -> rejected, a1 shares a diagonal
 4. Row 2: try c -> safe, place queen.            board: a1 c2
 5. Row 3: try a -> rejected, a1 shares the column
 6. Row 3: try b -> rejected, c2 shares a diagonal
 7. Row 3: try c -> rejected, a1 shares a diagonal
 8. Row 3: try d -> rejected, c2 shares a diagonal
 9. Row 2: nothing worked below c2, lift that queen      <- BACKTRACK
10. Row 2: try d -> safe, place queen.            board: a1 d2
11. Row 3: try a -> rejected, a1 shares the column
12. Row 3: try b -> safe, place queen.            board: a1 d2 b3
13. Row 4: try a -> rejected, a1 shares the column
14. Row 4: try b -> rejected, d2 shares a diagonal
15. Row 4: try c -> rejected, b3 shares a diagonal
16. Row 4: try d -> rejected, a1 shares a diagonal
17. Row 3: nothing worked below b3, lift that queen      <- BACKTRACK
18. Row 3: try c -> rejected, a1 shares a diagonal
19. Row 3: try d -> rejected, d2 shares the column
20. Row 2: nothing worked below d2, lift that queen      <- BACKTRACK
21. Row 1: nothing worked below a1, lift that queen      <- BACKTRACK
22. Row 1: try b -> safe, place queen.            board: b1

content.text: Steps 5 to 8 are the pattern in miniature. Every column in row 3 is attacked, so the loop finishes having placed nothing, and the call returns. That return
is
the backtrack: there is no special instruction for it, just a function running out of choices and handing control back to its caller.

Step 21 is the important one. After three nested backtracks the solver concludes that no arrangement at all begins with a queen on a1, and abandons that entire branch. Twenty steps of work have proved a single fact about the first row, and every one of those steps was necessary to prove it.
It reaches the first solution at step 31. Brute force over all 4-square placements would test 1,820 arrangements to get there.

content.text: The one-queen-per-row decision does not appear anywhere in the chart, because it is not a step. It is a choice about how the problem is represented, made before any code runs, and it is what turns "choose 8 squares from 64" into "choose a column for each row".
